food.text: In Scandinavia and northern Europe, some Subneolithic peoples (roughly 5000/4000 to 3200/2700 BCE) took up pottery from their farming neighbours but not farming itself. They kept living by hunting, gathering and fishing, and for the most part they were sedentary.

On the southeast Baltic coast, people at Šventoji and Benaičiai ate mostly freshwater fish, followed by seal and land animals. Scientists reached this conclusion by studying stable isotopes in human bones, fishing gear such as weirs and nets, and the numbers of bones from each species.

Coastal Subneolithic groups treated fishing as more than a way to eat, since it also appears in their folk art. Their fishing structures were impressive, even though gathering the wood for them took great effort. This suggests they relied heavily on aquatic resources for food.
Shortly after 4100 BCE the Ertebølle culture expanded along the Baltic coast at least as far as Rügen, and was soon afterwards replaced by the Funnelbeaker culture.

Refuse layers at Subneolithic sites show that pike was the most common freshwater fish. Rudd, bream, perch, zander and wels catfish were also eaten. Flounder and cod were the marine fish present, and the mammal bones came mostly from seal, along with boar, beaver and elk.

Analyses of wooden artefacts show that fishers at the Iijoki River used three methods of fishing. These included both active and passive techniques, which suggests a well-developed fishing tradition among Subneolithic groups.

Some sites as far north as Sweden were inhabited more than 10,000 years ago. This suggests that early hunter-gatherers may have used glacial termini as places from which to hunt migratory game such as reindeer.

Seal bones dominate the fragmentary remains at Subneolithic sites, but this partly reflects how easily they are identified. Fish bones are small and fragmented, and all parts of the fish were often used, so fish leave a smaller archaeological record than their real importance in the diet.

Some Subneolithic sites contain bones of domesticated animals and even grain, though keeping livestock was not a defining Subneolithic practice. Archaeologists take these finds as a sign of contact between Neolithic and Subneolithic cultures.

art.text: Around 4,000 BC the Funnel-beaker Culture brought farming to southern Scandinavia from the Continent. With it came monumental burial, polished flint axes and decorated pottery, giving the region some of its first shaped and ornamented objects on a large scale.

Within a century or two of the Funnel-beaker Culture's arrival, all of Denmark and the southern third of Sweden had become neolithised. Much of the area became dotted with megalithic tombs, making stone architecture a striking part of the landscape.

The Funnelbeaker culture, which lasted from about 4100 to 2800 BCE, used copper, especially for daggers and axes. It spread farming and husbandry to the pottery-using hunter-gatherers of southern Scandinavia and northern Germany.

In the later Ertebølle period, hunter-gatherer-fishers in Sweden lived in semi-permanent fishing settlements. They made pottery and buried their dead in large inhumation cemeteries, even though they still kept a Mesolithic way of life.

Mesolithic Scandinavia, divided into the Maglemosian, Kongemosian and Ertebølle Periods, was known for a microlithic flint technology. Where flint was not readily available, people worked quartz and slate instead.

Funnelbeaker sites of the 4th millennium BC have yielded artefacts of arsenical bronze. These were made using the lost-wax casting method, a sophisticated metalworking technique for such an early date.

Recent studies show the early copper used by the Funnelbeaker culture, from 4100 to 3000 BCE, was mined in Serbian and Bulgarian mines, not in the Austrian Alps as once believed. Copper artefacts became much rarer between 3300 and 2800 BCE, and are almost absent from 2800 to 2300 BCE.

war.text: When the Pitted Ware culture expanded across southern Scandinavia, the Funnelbeaker people built a number of defensive palisades. This may mean the two peoples were in conflict. Although they traded goods, they had widely different identities and did not mix to any notable extent.

There is archaeological evidence of high levels of violence among the people of the Pitted Ware culture. They were largely maritime hunters who lived along the coasts of Sweden, Denmark and southern Norway. Their culture lasted more than 1,000 years while remaining virtually unchanged.

The Battle Axe culture takes its name from the stone axes placed in graves beside the heads of men. About 3000 battle axes have been found across Scandinavia, though they are sparse in Norrland and northern Norway. They appear to have been status symbols.

The Kongemose culture of southern Scandinavia made long flint flakes into characteristic rhombic arrowheads. Tiny micro blades formed the edges of bone daggers, which were often decorated with geometric patterns. The culture lived from about 6000 BC to 5200 BC.

The Maglemosian culture used sharply edged flint microliths for spear and arrow heads. It flourished when sea levels were much lower and Scandinavia was linked to Britain through Doggerland. It also had a characteristic fishing spear called the leister.

Battle Axe graves were usually single flat graves without a barrow. Beyond the battle axes, grave goods included arrowheads, weapons of antler, amber beads, and polished flint axes and chisels. Around 250 such burials have been found in Sweden.

Some Funnelbeaker sites hold copper daggers and axes. Evidence for copper smelting in Scandinavia dates from c. 3500 BC. Studies show the early copper was mined in Serbian and Bulgarian mines, not in the Austrian Alps as once believed.

science.text: Ancient DNA shows that Mesolithic hunter-gatherers of Scandinavia were a blend of two older populations. Western hunter-gatherers first settled Scandinavia from the south, and eastern hunter-gatherers later entered from the north along the Norwegian coast. One study proposed an admixture ratio of about 65% western to 35% eastern.

Genomes of early Scandinavian hunter-gatherers show that a group from the south and another from the northeast eventually mixed in Scandinavia. The two groups differed in tool making as well as appearance. The southern population had darker skin and blue eyes, while the northern arrivals had light skin and variance in eye color.

Around 10,000 BC the rim of the ice was around Dalsland, Västergötland and Östergötland, and not until 7000 BC were all of Svealand and the northeastern coast free of ice. The huge weight of the ice sheet had caused isostatic depression of Fennoscandia, placing large parts of eastern Sweden and western Finland under water.

In a genetic study published in Nature Communications in January 2018, the remains of a hunter-gatherer female at Motala, Sweden, dated between 5750 BC and 5650 BC, were analyzed. She carried U5a2d and substantial ANE ancestry. The results supported the idea that these hunter-gatherers descended from a northward migration of western groups and a later southward migration of eastern ones.

Towards the end of the 4th millennium BC, the Nøstvet and Lihult tribes learnt new technology from the advancing farmers, but not agriculture, and became the Pitted Ware cultures. These Pitted Ware tribes halted the farmers' advance and pushed them south into southwestern Sweden, though some say the farmers were not killed or chased away but voluntarily joined the Pitted Ware culture. At least one settlement appears to be mixed, the Alvastra pile-dwelling.

Genetic studies found continuity between Scandinavian hunter-gatherers and members of the Pitted Ware culture of the Neolithic. Continuity was found only to a limited degree between those hunter-gatherers or the Pitted Ware culture and modern northern Europeans.

Genetic studies of the Kunda culture area found that around 3700/3600 BC there was a complete turnover to Y-haplogroup R1a1a1. From about 900/800 onward, mainly in Estonia, Y-haplogroup N-M231 had increasing impact.

Both light and dark skin pigmentation alleles were found at intermediate frequencies in the sampled Scandinavian hunter-gatherers. Only one individual had exclusively light-skin variants of two different SNPs.
Around 6200 BC the Ancylus age was followed by the formation of the Littorina Sea. Its stage, the Litorina Stage, is named after the Littorina littorea mollusc.

The 2018 study found that Mesolithic hunter-gatherers of the eastern Baltic carried high frequencies of the HERC2 allele, along with increased frequencies of the SLC45A2 and SLC24A5 alleles. They harbored less EHG ancestry than Scandinavian hunter-gatherers did.

A reconstruction of a late Scandinavian hunter-gatherer from about 7,000 years ago is displayed at Trelleborgs Museum in southern Sweden. His remains were found at the archaeological site of Skateholm, near Trelleborg.

politics.text: About 4000 BC, southern Scandinavia up to the River Dalälven in Sweden became part of the Funnelbeaker culture, which had originated in southern Europe. It replaced the Ertebølle culture, which had kept a Mesolithic lifestyle for about 1500 years after farming arrived in Central Europe.

The Comb Ceramic culture had a fairly extensive exchange network across the north. Finds include red slate from northern Scandinavia, asbestos from Lake Saimaa, green slate from Lake Onega, amber from the southern shores of the Baltic Sea and flint from the Valdai area in northwestern Russia.

The Pitted Ware culture emerged in east-central Sweden around 3,500 BC and gradually replaced the Funnelbeaker culture throughout the coastal areas of southern Scandinavia. Its people were a genetically homogeneous and distinct population descended from earlier Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers.

The Pitted Ware people were largely maritime hunters who traded animal goods with peoples throughout the Baltic. They were engaged in lively trade with the agricultural communities of the Scandinavian interior and with other hunter-gatherers of the Baltic Sea.

The Kunda culture appears to have grown out of the earlier Swiderian culture. The descendants of the Swiderians were evidently the first to settle Estonia once it became habitable, and the oldest known Kunda settlement in Estonia is Pulli.
Shortly after 4,100 BCE the Ertebølle culture began to expand along the Baltic coast, reaching at least as far as Rügen. Shortly after that it was replaced by the Funnelbeaker culture.

The Komsa people are thought to have followed the Norwegian coastline as receding glaciation opened up new areas for settlement. Some coastal sites in the Varangerfjord area, once attributed to the Komsa, actually represent an early incursion from northwestern Russia, related to the Post-Swiderian influx into Finnish Lapland.

Scholars debate what ethnicity the Narva culture represented, with Finno-Ugrians and other Europids both proposed. Both would precede the arrival of the Indo-Europeans, and it is unclear how the Narva culture fits with that arrival and the formation of the Baltic tribes.

culture.text: The Pitted Ware culture was a hunter-gatherer people living mainly along the coasts of southern Scandinavia. Although it is classed as Neolithic, it kept a Mesolithic economy even as farming reached the region. They were largely maritime hunters who traded with farming communities and with other Baltic hunter-gatherers.

The Pitted Ware people had an animistic cosmography, similar to that of the Comb Ceramic culture and other Mesolithic hunter-gatherers of the Baltic. Their spiritual world was shared across a wide hunting region rather than being unique to Scandinavia.

In the 7th millennium BC, forests had been established in Scandinavia after reindeer and their hunters moved north. Fire, boats and stone tools let Stone Age people survive there. Northern hunter-gatherers followed herds and salmon runs, moving south in winter and north in summer.

During the 5th millennium BC, the Ertebølle culture took up point-based pottery from human groups in the eastern Baltic, known as Narva. The Ertebølle had kept a Mesolithic lifestyle for about 1500 years after farming arrived in Central Europe.

When the Pitted Ware culture expanded, the Funnelbeakers built a number of defensive palisades, which may mean the two peoples were in conflict. The two exchanged goods but had widely different identities and did not mix much. There is also archaeological evidence of high levels of violence among the Pitted Ware people.

The Pitted Ware tribes halted the advance of the Funnelbeaker farmers and pushed them south into south-western Sweden. Some say the farmers were not killed or chased away but voluntarily joined the Pitted Ware culture and became part of them. At least one settlement appears to be mixed, the Alvastra pile-dwelling, where Funnelbeaker farmers and Pitted Ware people seem to have lived together.

At Flintbek in northern Germany, cart tracks from about 3400 BCE were found beneath a megalithic long barrow. They are the earliest known direct evidence of wheeled vehicles in the world, not just models or images.

Funnelbeaker people practiced copper metallurgy, and evidence for copper smelting in Scandinavia dates from about 3500 BC. Their early copper was mined in Serbian and Bulgarian mines, not the Austrian Alps as once believed.

In the Funnelbeaker culture, houses were centered on a monumental grave, which served as a symbol of social cohesion. Burial practices varied by region and changed over time, though inhumation seems to have been the rule.
